newsitem.title: USA: USAir proposed low-cost initiative - source.
newsitem.headline: USAir proposed low-cost initiative - source.

text.p: As part of USAir Group Inc's massive turnaround efforts, the airline has asked its pilots union to approve a plan for a new low-cost unit to compete with rivals such as Southwest Airlines Co, a source familiar with the discussions said.

USAir and its pilots declined to comment on the proposal presented to the pilots union this week, which calls for USAir to convert up to 40 percent of its flying time or block hours into a new, low-cost operation.
But the airline and the pilots have previously said they were discussing options for low-cost service.
USAir and the pilots are now at odds about the size of the low-cost operation, the routes it would fly and the pay rates for those workers, the source said.

USAir wants the pilots who fly with the new operation, which is internally referred to as "US2," to earn less than those on the main carrier, to fly more hours and to receive less vacation and sick-leave benefits, the source said.
The company also wants US2 to fly on all route up to 1,000 miles and certain routes up to 1,600 miles, the source said.
The pilots union supports the development of US2, but on a smaller scale, the source said.
The pilots offered a counterproposal, saying US2 should account for only 10 percent of USAir's block hours and fly on routes of less than 1,000 miles, the source said.
The pilots also rejected management's proposal for less pay for US2 pilots.
The union proposed that USAir pay rates comparable to Southwest's wage structure and recall some of its furloughed pilots to fly US2 routes, the source said.
While talks between USAir and the union are preliminary, USAir will likely launch the low-cost unit this year, said the source, who is familiar with the talks.
The pilots union first approached the company about developing a low-cost unit three years ago. This fall, USAir and the union began discussing specific options.
Developing a low-cost unit is a crucial part of USAir's efforts to reduce operating costs, which are among the highest in the industry, analysts said.
USAir faces increasing pressure from the aggressive expansion of Southwest Airlines and the initial success of Delta Air Lines Inc's new express unit.
But a low-cost operation can be a risky gamble -- other airlines have fumbled with these efforts in the past, analysts said.
The new unit would reduce costs and ease USAir's efforts in obtaining financing for its order for 400 Airbus Industrie aircraft.
The airline previously said the aircraft order is contingent on first achieving a "competitive cost structure." The first jets are expected to begin delivery in 1998.
